lesson.title: The Starting Point That Is Not Always Real
lesson.summary: The y-intercept is the model's predicted response when the explanatory variable equals zero, but that number is only meaningful when zero is a realistic, observed value of x.
lesson.body:
The intercept of a regression equation, b0, is the model's predicted value of the response variable when the explanatory variable equals exactly zero, the point where the line would cross the vertical axis if it were extended that far. It is read directly off the equation without any extra calculation: it is simply the constant term sitting by itself.

In the worked example, b0 equals 39, so the model predicts an exam score of 39 for a student who studied 0 hours. That is a mathematically valid reading of the equation, produced by the exact same formula used for every other point on the line, but whether it means anything in the real world depends entirely on context, and that check is where most errors happen.

The observed hours studied in this data set ranged only from 1 to 5. Zero hours was never actually observed among the five students used to fit the line, so the prediction of 39 points is not describing anything that actually happened, it is extending the line beyond the data that were used to build it in the first place. Students who study zero hours might behave completely differently from the pattern seen among students who studied at least one hour, perhaps guessing randomly on every question, perhaps having unusual background knowledge from a previous class, so treating 39 as a solid real world claim would be a mistake. This exact situation, trusting a prediction outside the range of the original data, gets its own full treatment in the coming chapter on extrapolation.

Contrast this with a case where the intercept is fully meaningful and not an extrapolation at all. Suppose a biologist measures a seedling's height in centimeters every day over the first ten days after it sprouts, with day 0 genuinely included among the observed data collected. Here, the intercept represents the seedling's actual height at day zero, a real, observed, and interpretable quantity, not an extrapolation beyond the data. The difference between the two examples is never the math, both intercepts are computed by the identical formula, it is entirely whether x equal to zero sits inside the range of data that was actually collected.

Even when x equal to zero is technically inside or near the observed range, an intercept can still be a weaker description than it looks if very few data points were actually collected near that value. The line's behavior anywhere is best supported where the data are dense, typically near the mean of x, and least supported near the edges of the observed range, so an intercept resting right at the edge deserves a bit more caution than a prediction made nearer the center of the data.

Before reporting any intercept as a real world fact, two questions are always worth asking: is x equal to zero a value that could realistically occur for this variable at all, and was that value, or values reasonably close to it, actually present in the data used to fit the line. Only when both answers are yes does the intercept deserve a literal, real world interpretation.
